title: Assessing context-dependent effectiveness of heat adaptation through human mobility under different heatwave regimes
abstract: As heatwaves intensify under climate change, cities increasingly rely on adaptation strategies to mitigate risk. Yet, the real-world effectiveness of climate adaptation measures in influencing human behavior to support daily functioning across cities remains limited. Using daily intracity mobility data aggregated from over 1.1 billion mobile devices across 366 Chinese cities in 2023, we apply a causal inference framework based on causal random forest to quantify the heterogeneous effects of three key adaptation measures: access to cooling centers, urban greenness (NDVI), and heat warnings during daytime-only and compound day-night heatwaves. We find that the adaptation effectiveness varies markedly by heatwave type and local socioeconomic conditions. Public cooling facilities reduced mobility during daytime-only heatwaves but promoted it under day-night heatwaves, especially in low GDP per capita, aging and agriculturally dependent cities. In contrast, greenness consistently failed to sustain mobility in elderly or agriculturally dominant cities. Heat warnings exhibited paradoxical effects: although intended to discourage heat exposure, they were often associated with increased mobility at extreme temperatures in vulnerable cities, while showing only modest suppressive effects in younger, less agricultural cities. These findings reveal that the benefits of adaptation are highly context-dependent and unequally distributed, highlighting the need for precision adaptation: strategies tailored not only to environmental conditions but also to behavioral, demographic, and socioeconomic variability. By linking adaptation measures to near real-time behavioral responses, our study offers a scalable, data-driven framework to guide more equitable and effective urban climate-resilient planning.

title: Assessing social equity and urban heat risks with machine learning of remote sensing imagery: A Pittsburgh case study
abstract: Rapid urban development has intensified soil sealing by impervious surfaces, contributing to extreme urban heat, flooding, and health risks. Although research on the impact of impervious surfaces on urban heat has grown in recent years, most studies overlook variations in surface characteristics, such as surface color, which influence urban heat. Consequently, city-wide data on sub-categorized impervious surfaces remain limited. This research fills this gap by using high-resolution remote-sensing imagery classification in ArcGIS Pro to map surface characteristics in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and examine their relationship with land surface temperatures (LST) and social vulnerability. Results show that impervious surfaces cover 55% of the city, including 22% roofs, 30.7% roads and 2.3% parking lots, with 52% of these surfaces classified as dark. On average, historically redlined neighborhoods are 2.6 °C (4.7 °F) hotter and contain a higher proportion of dark surfaces. These results underscore the role of surface color and composition in shaping urban thermal inequities and emphasize the need for evidence-based decision-making in surface material selection to build more equitable and sustainable cities. • Pittsburgh’s overall roofs, streets, and parking lots are 52% dark. • Summer surface temperatures can reach 68.6 °C (155.4 °F). • Historically redlined neighborhoods have 12.6% more dark surfaces and are 2.6 °C (4.7°F) hotter. • Each 1% more dark surface adds 0.18 °C (0.32 °F) to summer LST. • Dark and light surfaces show modest correlations with SVI across Pittsburgh.

title: Urban flood susceptibility decoded: A GeoAI workflow for urban flood-prone area delineation and mitigation mechanism inference
abstract: Under the combined pressures of intensified extreme rainfall and accelerating impervious urban expansion, pluvial flooding has emerged as a dominant threat to urban safety and sustainability. Conventional flood-susceptibility models have faced challenges in handling highly sparse, long-tailed target distributions and in providing physical interpretability, which has limited the fine-scale delineation of flood-prone cells and the development of differentiated mitigation strategies. To address this issue, an integrated GeoAI-based framework was developed to systematically links urban surface characteristics with socio-hydrological processes for advancing flood-risk governance. The proposed framework synthesizes 25 natural and socio-economic variables to holistically capture flood-generation mechanisms across diverse city contexts. Through a two-stage feature distillation process, the ten most critical drivers shaping flood susceptibility in each city were identified. These drives underpin a novel zero-inflated convolutional self-attention network (ZI-Geo-CNN), which generated high-resolution susceptibility maps for six major Chinese cities with exceptional accuracy ( R 2 > 0.98 , A U C ≈ 1.00 , and S M A P E < 13 % ) . Post‑hoc analysis using Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) quantified each driver’s relative contribution, revealing universal controls alongside economy–infrastructure couplings. Based on shared and differentiated patterns of factor importance across cities, this study compared dominant patterns across cities and discussed several indicative adaptation directions. Overall, the framework breaks the accuracy–interpretability trade-off for sparse, long-tailed flood data and furnishes a replicable GeoAI workflow that can be applied consistently across cities through city-specific training, calibration, and interpretation, thereby providing an evidence-informed basis for resilient drainage planning under non-stationary climates.

title: Beyond sensing: AI-Driven planning paradigm shifts for sustainable development
abstract: Urban complexity represents one of the most significant challenges for sustainable development in the AI era. Traditional planning methods often struggle to navigate their dynamic and complex nature. Drawing upon the "Urban Iceberg" theoretical framework, we launch the special issue “Integrating AI into Sustainable Urban Development: Planning Approaches and Strategies.” The studies published in this issue provide robust evidence that AI has matured into a powerful tool for decoding the visible physical city environment through high-precision sensing and pattern optimization. However, building truly sustainable cities necessitates penetrating the submerged social environment—the domain of conflicting values, institutional logic, and human needs. This demands a structural transition from observing physical phenomena to decoding underlying socio-economic mechanisms. We advocate for the advancement of cognitive AI to simulate stakeholder negotiation and facilitate human-AI co-creation. This special issue serves not only as a repository of technical advances but as a roadmap for bridging the divide between physical intelligence and social rationality. Only by integrating these dimensions can we transform AI from a tool of measurement into an instrument of humane and sustainable development.

title: Declining thermal walkability in the Arabian Peninsula: a thermal-climate analysis with walking implications
abstract: Walking benefits both physical and mental health. Arabian Peninsula, as one of the regions with highest physical inactivity rates, faces significant barriers to outdoor walking due to the extreme hot climate. This study defined thermal walkability as whether thermal conditions support outdoor walking based on a thermal index, modified Physiologically Equivalent Temperature, and investigated its spatial and temporal (both seasonal and diurnal) distribution and long-term trends across the Arabian Peninsula over the period 1986–2024. The results showed a pronounced seasonal contrast: October–April features widespread thermally walkable conditions for most non-sleeping hours, with little decadal change; while summer and transitional months experienced poor thermal walkability, with thermally walkable hours mainly around sunrise and after sunset, and the probability of thermal walkability during these periods was declining significantly. The meteorological drivers of thermally unwalkable conditions for four major cities were identified based on the results of logistic regression and random forest models. Air temperature and solar radiation turned out to be the primary determinants while wind velocity and vapour pressure have weak effects across hot-arid to hot-humid climates. These findings highlight the necessity for region- and time-specific mitigation and adaptation strategies against the reduced thermal walkability and offer valuable references for policymakers to create supportive environments for outdoor walking.

title: A cross-city analysis of mobility responses to air pollution in China
abstract: • We identify causal effects of air pollution on within-city mobility in China. • PM2.5 poses an average negative causal impact on within-city mobility in China. • There are substantial spatial variations underlying the PM2.5-mobility nexus. • Positive effects are observed in some cities. • The spatial heterogeneities are mainly driven by pollution and mobility levels. Understanding how air quality influences mobility patterns is crucial for effective transport and environmental management. While existing studies have explored the mobility impacts of air pollution, their findings remain inconsistent, partly due to the dualistic mobility responses (increased population redistribution within the city and reduced mobility for pollution avoidance) during high-pollution episodes. Here, we examine the causal effect of PM 2.5 levels on within-city mobility and explore driving factors of the spatial heterogeneity underlying this effect across 318 Chinese cities from May to November 2023, employing econometric models and explainable machine learning techniques. We find that, on average, a one-standard-deviation (16.99 μg/m 3 ) increase in PM 2.5 level reduces daily trips by approximately 0.28-0.41%, reflecting widespread travel avoidance on heavily polluted days. However, mobility responses exhibit significant spatial heterogeneity. Among sample cities, a negative association between air pollution and mobility has been observed in 68% of them, with the rest suggesting the other way around. The explainable machine learning model results further reveal that this disparity is mainly driven by transboundary air pollution and long-term mobility levels, sociodemographic factors (e.g., age, population, and tertiary industry GDP share), as well as land use features (e.g., population density, geographical area of the city). Our findings offer a scientific basis for continued air pollution mitigation efforts and support the design of targeted land use policies tailored to local conditions.

title: From heat maps to cooling actions: AI-driven citywide hourly mapping of thermal stress, drivers, and targeted cooling
abstract: • MLP-ANN fuses weather and morphology to predict hourly NET across Hong Kong. • Model achieves R²=0.97, resolving diurnal and seasonal thermal stress patterns. • Summer NET peaks at 30.29°C (15:00); winter nights drop to -4.02°C (03:00). • Elevated NET concentrates in highly urbanized zones (e.g., airport, CBD). • Larger green and water patches provide the strongest localized cooling effects. Thermal stress is critical for sustainable, health-oriented urban planning, yet remains difficult to characterize at hourly resolution and citywide in dense cities. Using Hong Kong as a case study, this study develops a regression-based machine learning framework to predict hourly thermal stress, expressed as Net Effective Temperature (NET). Long-term meteorological data was combined with detailed geographic, urban-morphological, and landscape composition–configuration metrics in a multilayer perceptron artificial neural network (MLP-ANN). The model uses 37 input variables, while the target variable is the continuous hourly NET. The model attains high predictive skill (R² = 0.97, RMSE=1.1°C over the full dataset) and captures pronounced diurnal and seasonal patterns in thermal stress. Performance remains robust under hot (R² = 0.97, RMSE = 0.5°C) and cold (R² = 0.94, RMSE = 1.7°C) conditions. In summer, afternoon NET reaches about 30.3°C and remains elevated at night, whereas in winter nocturnal NET can fall below –4°C. Spatially, higher NET concentrates in dense urban and industrial districts, with summer hotspots around the airport, Northwest New Territories, and Kwai Tsing Container Terminals. Daytime NET is dominated by near-surface air temperature, followed by P impervious and NDBI, along with configuration metrics such as SHAPE, CIRCLE, and AREA, while P green and NDWI become especially influential in winter daytime. At night, configuration metrics including FRAC, CONTIG, CORE, and GYRATE gain importance. The framework delivers citywide, hourly NET maps and quantitative driver rankings to guide targeted, nature-based and morphological interventions in subtropical high-density cities.

title: Optimizing the green-grey ratio: Nonlinear effects of urban form on PM2.5 in mid-sized cities
abstract: • Green-Grey Ratio defines air quality resilience in mid-sized cities. • Green infrastructure efficacy reveals a thermal tipping point at 19°C. • Intermediate Green-Grey ratios (0.8–1.2) minimize PM2.5 during heat. • Excessive vegetation density can trap pollution by reducing ventilation. • Mid-sized cities require heat-adaptive zoning, not static greening. Urban greening is widely promoted as a strategy to mitigate particulate air pollution and urban heat island, yet its effectiveness varies across climatic conditions. This study examines whether urban greening exhibits a temperature-dependent threshold in influencing PM₂.₅ concentrations in a mid-sized Midwestern city representative of temperate urban regions. Using high-frequency air-quality observations integrated with gridded urban morphology data, we analyze how the balance between green and built infrastructure, captured by a Green–Grey Ratio, interacts with temperature to shape PM₂.₅ variability. Results reveal a nonlinear relationship in which PM₂.₅ concentrations are lowest at intermediate green–grey balances, but only under warm conditions. Below approximately 19–20°C, PM₂.₅ variability is dominated by meteorological factors and combustion indicators, and urban greening shows limited influence. Above this threshold, vegetation and urban form increasingly modulate baseline PM₂.₅ levels and the likelihood of extreme pollution events. Random Forest analysis corroborates this transition, indicating higher relative importance of vegetation metrics during warm periods. The key novelty is demonstrating that greening benefits for PM₂.₅ are non-monotonic and temperature-contingent, with an intermediate Green–Grey “optimum” and a warm-regime tipping point that has direct implications for heat-resilient urban design. These findings suggest that optimizing the balance between green and built infrastructure requires accounting for climatic context and nonlinearity, with implications for urban design and air-quality management in mid-sized cities.

title: Physics-informed machine learning for mapping the heat mitigation potential of vegetation in Singapore
abstract: This study develops a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) model using a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to estimate vegetation cooling effects, specifically spatially averaged air temperature reduction (ΔT) and vegetation-surrounding UTCI reduction (ΔUTCI), across heterogeneous urban contexts. The model incorporates building, vegetation, and climate features and is trained on ENVI-met simulations from 22 representative sites in Singapore, covering monsoon and inter-monsoon scenarios. These sites, selected through context-based mapping, capture diverse building and greenery configurations. By embedding physics constraints on sensible and latent heat fluxes from the Surface Energy Balance into the loss function, the model captures the overall influence of vegetation at the pedestrian level (2 m), with the physics loss enhancing accuracy and generalizability. A sensitivity analysis and an explanatory study using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are conducted to assess the local and global impacts of features. The contributions of building, vegetation, and climate features to vegetation cooling effects are quantified across day/night and monsoon/inter-monsoon seasons. Results indicate that during daytime, ΔT is largely influenced by vegetation features (40%), whereas ΔUTCI is primarily driven by background climate features (47%), with seasonal variations affecting individual feature importance. These insights inform scenario-based urban design guidelines for optimizing vegetation cooling potential. The trained model is applied to built-up areas in Singapore, generating a vegetation cooling distribution map that reveals a mean ΔT of 0.5 °C and a mean ΔUTCI of 2 °C across all sites around noon. Targeted interventions are proposed for areas with suboptimal vegetation cooling performance, providing an urban design solution for leveraging greenery as a passive cooling strategy to mitigate urban heat in high-density cities.

title: Can transit-oriented development (TOD) cool the city? A multi-scale geospatial assessment of daytime surface heat exposure in Tokyo
abstract: Extreme heat and heat-related illness are increasing in urban environments, underscoring the need for design strategies that improve pedestrian thermal comfort. Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) is widely promoted as a sustainable urban model, yet its climatic implications remain unclear. This study examines whether, and under what conditions, TOD can mitigate heat exposure, using Shinjuku City in Tokyo as a case study. We develop an XGBoost model trained on multimodal data, integrating urban form indicators from street-level imagery, population estimates, and open-source built-environment metrics. Land surface temperature (LST) responses to TOD spatial configurations are interpreted using Partial Dependence Plots and SHAP values. Contrary to studies suggesting that TOD exacerbates urban heat through high density and limited vegetation, our results indicate that well-designed TOD corridors can yield measurable cooling effects. TOD areas characterized by dense rail infrastructure, vertically integrated building morphology, and accessible public space exhibit LST values up to 0.9 °C below the citywide mean. However, this benefit is conditional: station-centered hubs lacking continuous corridor connectivity, shading, or permeable surfaces often emerge as local hotspots. Vegetation cover, mixed land use, and pedestrian accessibility consistently reduce LST, whereas excessive building or population density without mitigating design elements intensifies heat exposure. We conclude that TOD acts not as a uniform solution but as a spatial moderator of thermal heterogeneity, whose performance depends on how transport infrastructure and urban form are co-designed. This study contributes to pioneering efforts that empirically examine TOD–heat interactions using explainable machine learning, providing evidence to guide heat-resilient transit planning.

title: When does AI become worth it? A multi-attribute utility perspective for urban climate planning
abstract: Urban climate modeling is essential for resilient city planning but remains constrained by high computational costs and expert dependence. We introduce KLIMASCANNER, an AI-based QGIS plugin for rapid microclimate predictions, and employ Multi-Attribute Utility Theory (MAUT) to compare it against conventional case-by-case (CBC) modeling across five dimensions: energy efficiency, speed, transparency, cost, and accuracy. Monte Carlo analysis (N=10,000) with three uncertainty sources shows KLIMASCANNER is preferred in 94–99.9% of scenarios depending on stakeholder profile, with break-even at approximately 40 simulations. Sensitivity analyses confirm robustness to cost assumptions and weight configurations, though CBC remains competitive when transparency is prioritized. AI-assisted modeling can democratize urban climate assessment for smaller municipalities, while numerical outputs alone cannot fully capture decision-making complexity in climate-resilient planning. • KLIMASCANNER is an AI-based QGIS plugin that predicts how urban developments affect local temperature, wind fields, cold air corridors, and thermal comfort indices at 5 m resolution. • Multi-Attribute Utility Theory (MAUT) with Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis (N=10,000) provides a rigorous framework to compare AI-based and physics-based climate modeling approaches. • KLIMASCANNER is preferred in 94–99.9% of simulated scenarios, depending on stakeholder profile, with citizens showing the highest uncertainty due to transparency considerations. • Break-even analysis indicates AI-based tools become cost-effective after approximately 40 simulations, democratizing climate assessment for smaller municipalities.

title: Interpretable modelling of private electric vehicles adoption in Ireland: Bridging forecasts and policy
abstract: The adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) is a central pathway to reducing road transport emissions and meeting international climate goals. This study develops a two-phase hybrid forecasting and explainability framework to model private EV adoption in Ireland, while accounting for economic conditions, energy prices, policy signals, and public awareness. In the first phase, a Manta Ray Foraging Optimization–Variational Mode Decomposition–Residual Gated Recurrent Unit (MRFO VMD ResGRU) framework is employed to generate multi-horizon forecasts of monthly private EV registrations at 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month leads. The VMD-based signal decomposition separates trend, seasonal, and high-frequency components. Each temporal scale is then modeled through the ResGRU architecture, which results in stronger short-, medium-, and long-horizon performance than other models from the same recurrent network family. In the second phase, a surrogate-based explainable learning strategy applies SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) through an Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model that mimics the MRFO-VMD-ResGRU forecasts. The explainability analysis identifies annual average wage and the Google Trends Index (GTI), as a proxy for public interest, as the most influential factors associated with private EV adoption, followed by fuel prices. Higher income levels, stronger public interest, and higher petrol prices are positively associated with EV adoption, whereas, interestingly, higher diesel prices exhibit a negative association with uptake. This hybrid time series forecasting strategy with explainable AI gives policymakers and stakeholders transparent, data-driven insights that guide planning for private vehicle electrification and the achievement of long-term emission reduction targets in Ireland.

title: The next frontier of generative intelligence in smarter eco-cities: A systematic review of deep generative and hybrid modeling applications for environmental sustainability
abstract: • Provides the first cross-domain systematic synthesis of generative, hybrid, and mixed architectures for smarter eco-city intelligence. • Reveals distinct functional roles of GANs, VAEs, DMs, and transformers across urban–environmental systems. • Identifies a methodological shift from standalone models to integrated, multi-layered architectures enabling cross-system intelligence. • Proposes a novel hierarchical conceptual framework linking model capabilities to urban–ecological applications and decision-making layers. • Highlights technical and architectural constraints, data-related barriers, environmental and computational costs, and ethical and societal limitations Recent advancements in GenAI have gained increasing prominence, unveiling transformative opportunities to reconceptualize, analyze, manage, and plan urban–ecological systems. This development aligns with the emerging paradigm of smarter eco-cities, which function as experimental environments for testing and scaling technological innovations and environmental reforms. Despite the growing interest in applying GenAI to environmental sustainability and smart cities in recent years, the existing literature remains fragmented, domain-specific, and largely exploratory, often focusing on isolated use cases, individual model types, or narrowly defined functional areas. To the best of our knowledge, no review has systematically examined how Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), Diffusion Models (DMs), Transformers, and hybrid and mixed architectures can be adapted to the operational and strategic demands of smarter eco-cities. This study addresses this gap by providing the first systematic, cross-domain review of state-of-the-art applications of deep generative, hybrid, and mixed modeling for advancing environmental sustainability goals in smarter eco-cities. Methodologically, it synthesizes evidence from 145 studies through a unified framework that integrates aggregative, configurative, tabulated, and narrative approaches. Findings reveal that these modeling architectures advance generative, predictive, adaptive, and integrative intelligence across multiple urban–environmental domains, including energy systems, renewable energy, decarbonization, buildings, mobility and transport, waste and wastewater, air quality, carbon capture, water and hydrology, biodiversity and ecosystems, as well as disaster response and climate resilience. GANs excel in high-fidelity scenario realism and data augmentation; VAEs offer probabilistic interpretability, uncertainty modeling, and data imputation; DMs specialize in stable, controllable, and physically consistent simulations of complex spatiotemporal systems; Transformers enable multimodal temporal reasoning and long-range dependency modeling; and hybrid and mixed architectures combine these strengths or integrate them with discriminative, deterministic, heuristic, and/or symbolic components to support multifunctional, cross-system solutions. Building on these insights, the study proposes a novel conceptual framework that hierarchically integrates deep generative, hybrid, and mixed modeling approaches to advance smarter eco-city intelligence. However, persistent challenges remain, including technical and architectural constraints, hallucinations and epistemic uncertainty, data-related barriers, environmental and computational costs, and ethical and societal limitations, all of which hinder responsible and sustainable deployment. The findings carry significant implications for urban planners, researchers, and policymakers, highlighting the need for transdisciplinary collaboration, standardized evaluation frameworks across domains, and guidance for operationalizing urban-ecological intelligence strategies while ensuring ethical and inclusive implementation.

title: Urban greening, heat resilience, and economic activity in city cores: Evidence from 12 heat-vulnerable global cities using spatial double machine learning
abstract: • Finds a robust positive NDVI effect on nighttime lights in 12 city cores • Proposes spatial double machine learning with MLP/GNN nuisance learning • Decomposes direct and thermal-mediated effects with cluster-bootstrap inference • Indirect cooling mediation is model-sensitive and insignificant under GNN-DML • Shows spatial neighbourhood spillovers and clustered impacts on local activities Urban greening is widely promoted as a nature-based solution for heat adaptation, yet evidence on its economic co-benefits in dense urban cores remains limited and may be biased by nonlinearity and spatial dependence. This study proposes a spatial causal framework to estimate how urban-core greenery relates to fine-scale economic activity intensity, proxied by VIIRS Black Marble nighttime lights, across 12 heat-vulnerable cities (Bangkok, Cairo, Delhi, Doha, Dubai, Jakarta, Las Vegas, Manila, Mumbai, Phoenix, Singapore, Tokyo) from 2013-2024 using a polygon-year panel and a morphology-based urban-core boundary procedure. We apply double machine learning with city and year fixed effects and harmonized Earth-observation remote sensing covariates (NDVI, land surface temperature, built-up and moisture indices, and population), comparing non-spatial multilayer perceptron learners to graph neural network learners that explicitly encode polygon adjacency. Results show a robust positive association between greenery and nighttime lights in urban cores, with estimated total and direct effects remaining positive under spatially robust specifications. Mechanism analysis via causal mediation indicates that the cooling-mediated component is sensitive to spatial modelling: it appears significant under non-spatial learners but becomes statistically indistinguishable from zero when spatial dependence is absorbed by graph-based nuisance learning, consistent with neighbourhood-scale cooling spillovers and spatially structured confounding. Spatial spillover models further show that neighbouring greenness and neighbouring heat exposure meaningfully relate to local outcomes. These findings support spatially aware evaluation of greening strategies in heat-vulnerable urban settings and suggest that urban sustainability policies should consider both amenity-driven and heat-resilience pathways when targeting interventions in dense city centres. The results should be interpreted within the climatic scope of the sample and may not directly generalize to temperate-city contexts.

title: The ‘What If’ framework: A scenario-based counterfactual approach to modelling urban resilience and disaster impact
abstract: Urban growth in hazard-prone regions is frequently shaped by informal settlement expansion. Yet, disaster impact assessments typically evaluate only observed post-event conditions and do not consider how urban development trajectories might have evolved in the absence of disruptive events. This study applies a counterfactual modelling approach (‘What-If’ framework) that integrates deep learning–based multi-temporal land-cover mapping with Cellular Automata (CA) simulation to analyse alternative urban development pathways. The framework is implemented in Mocoa, Colombia, following the 2017 debris-flow disaster. Multi-temporal land-cover maps were generated using a U-Net deep learning architecture and used to calibrate and compare three CA modelling frameworks: Land Change Modeler (LCM), MOLUSCE, and the Geographic Automata Tool (GAT). Model performance was evaluated using a two-stage validation strategy designed to test sensitivity to the temporal representativeness of calibration data. Global agreement metrics (Overall Accuracy, Cohen’s Kappa, and Figure of Merit) and class-specific metrics (Precision, Recall, F1-Score, and Intersection over Union) were calculated, with particular focus on the ‘Informal Built-up’ class. Results indicate that models trained only on incremental growth patterns (2010–2013) showed limited ability to reproduce informal settlement emergence observed in 2016, whereas calibration including the spontaneous growth phase (2010–2016) substantially improved predictive performance. Among the tested frameworks, LCM achieved the highest class-specific performance (F1-Score = 94.34%, IoU = 89.29%). The counterfactual simulation for 2021 suggests that, without the disaster, informal settlements would have expanded by approximately 1.68 ha into hazard-exposed areas, indicating continued exposure accumulation under pre-disaster growth dynamics. The results demonstrate how counterfactual urban simulations can complement conventional disaster assessments by quantifying differences between observed and alternative development trajectories, providing a basis for evaluating long-term spatial implications of disruptive events.

title: Physics-informed neural network calibration and application for urban cooling
abstract: Mitigating the adverse effects of urban heat islands (UHI) is essential for enhancing climate resilience, public health, and energy sustainability in cities. Traditional modelling approaches, however, often face a trade-off between physical fidelity and the flexibility to integrate diverse geospatial data. This paper presents a novel physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework that bridges this gap by embedding the heat diffusion equation directly into a neural network, ensuring predictions adhere to thermodynamic principles while learning from complex urban data patterns. It includes a systematic data-fusion workflow that unifies multi-format geospatial inputs, such as land surface temperature (LST), vegetation indices, and vector-based urban morphology, into a cohesive gridded structure, enabling scalable and reproducible urban climate analysis. Validated through a case study of Paris, the model achieves strong predictive accuracy (MAE=0.3723 °C, RMSE = 0.5019 °C) and captures the city’s thermal patterns with consistent error across the observed temperature range. Comparing two targeting metrics, LST and the proposed urban heat thermal index (UHTI), shows that LST favors areas with some existing vegetation while UHTI identifies more barren, structurally vulnerable zones. Simulated green roof deployment on buildings selected by each metric yields localised surface cooling up to 4.97 °C, concentrated on the building footprints. This integrated approach thus serves as a practical scenario planning tool, quantifying the relative benefits of green infrastructure. By combining physical simulation with data-driven analytics, this research provides urban planners and policymakers with a scientifically rigorous, scalable resource to support the design of cooler, and more sustainable cities.

title: What heats cosmopolitan cities in summer? A remote sensing and AI study of land surface temperature drivers: Casablanca vs Barcelona
abstract: Urbanization and climate change are increasingly intensifying the urban heat island effect, especially during summer, by changing the relationship between land cover and local thermal conditions. This study investigates how five environmental indicators (NDVI, NDMI, NDBI, NDBSI, and albedo) influence land surface temperature (LST) across Local Climate Zones (LCZs) in two cities with contrasting climates and urban forms, Casablanca and Barcelona, during the summer period (July 1–August 31) from 2014 to 2024. Landsat 8 imagery and the WUDAPT database were combined with seven machine-learning regression models. Among these, the Extra Trees Regressor demonstrated the strongest performance, achieving the highest R² values (0.96–0.98 in training and 0.59–0.85 in testing), the lowest error metrics, and the best bias, and was therefore selected to assess the contribution of each predictor by LCZ class and year. Results show that vegetation, represented by NDVI, plays a leading role in regulating LST in Barcelona, with the highest feature importance values (0.30–0.40), consistent with its Mediterranean setting. In Casablanca, thermal variability is more strongly associated with urbanization-related indicators, particularly NDBI and NDBSI, with feature importance reaching 0.57. In addition, Barcelona exhibits a statistically significant upward trend in summer LST, with mean Sen’s slopes of 0.31°C/year in built LCZs and 0.34°C/year in land-cover LCZs, according to the Mann–Kendall test. Casablanca shows a comparatively more stable thermal pattern. These findings highlight that LST–environment relationships depend on both LCZ structure and regional climate, providing insights for urban heat mitigation and climate-adaptation strategies.

title: Differentiated street greenery cooling of road surfaces: Spatially varying nonlinear effects from street view and geographically weighted machine learning
abstract: Urban vegetation is a critical nature-based solution for mitigating the urban heat island effect, yet its cooling efficacy on road surfaces varies spatially due to differences in vegetation type, structure, and local urban morphology. This study investigates the spatially varying nonlinear cooling effects of differentiated street greenery, including trees, shrubs, and grass, on land surface temperature (LST) using Google Street View (GSV) imagery in Zurich, Switzerland. A fine-tuned Mask2Former deep learning model was employed for semantic segmentation to accurately extract five street view factors (trees, shrubs, grass, buildings, and sky) from GSV images collected via three methods: multi-view collection, panoramic image collection, and fisheye. These factors were then compared across methods, revealing methodological biases but limited influence on subsequent modeling outcomes. A geographically weighted random forest model integrated with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis was developed to capture spatially non-stationary and nonlinear relationships between the five view factors and LST derived from Landsat 8. Results show that trees exert the strongest nonlinear cooling effect, followed by shrubs, while grass provides moderate and context-dependent benefits; buildings consistently drive warming, and sky view has minimal impact. The three GSV collection methods yield comparable predictive performance and feature interpretations, suggesting practical flexibility in method selection. This framework advances street-level urban climate research by combining pedestrian-perspective data with local machine learning interpretability, offering evidence-based insights for targeted greening strategies in heat-vulnerable urban areas.

title: Machine learning for urban wind simulation: A comprehensive review
abstract: Urban wind simulation plays an important role in pedestrian comfort assessment, wind safety evaluation, air quality analysis, and broader urban environmental planning. Conventional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) approaches, although physically grounded, remain computationally demanding and highly reliant on mesh quality, which makes them impractical for large-scale or iterative urban design workflows. This study reviews recent developments in data-driven, physics-informed, and hybrid machine learning methods for urban wind prediction, with attention to their modeling assumptions, validation strategies, and generalization behavior. The literature is organized along the urban wind simulation pipeline to provide a structured overview of current surrogate modeling approaches and their practical limitations. The review highlights open challenges related to robustness, benchmarking, and uncertainty quantification, and discusses directions for improving the reliability and scalability of ML-based urban wind modeling.

title: Quantifying the impacts of urban form on air pollution using Local Climate Zone classifications in Greater London: a machine learning approach
abstract: Urban air pollution remains a persistent challenge for global cities. The Local Climate Zone (LCZ) framework, which classifies urban environments based on land cover, physical geometry, and thermal properties, has shown significant potential for air pollution research. However, few studies have quantitatively explored the relationship between air pollution and LCZs. To address this gap, the study combines ultra-high-resolution pollutant concentration data (PM 2.5 , PM 10 , NO 2 , NO x ; grid size 20m × 20m) with LCZs (grid size 100m × 100m) and applies interpretable machine learning models. The Extreme Gradient Boosting algorithm, combined with the SHapley Additive exPlanations is used. Findings from Greater London show that the trained machine learning model incorporating LCZ categories, spatial coordinates, and buffer features provides strong performance, with testing R² of 0.89 for PM 2.5 , 0.85 for PM 10 , 0.90 for NO 2 , and 0.82 for NO x . The most polluted LCZs (the three highest deviations above the overall average) are concentrated within only 3.82% of Greater London. These include LCZ1 (Compact highrise), LCZ2 (Compact midrise), LCZ10 (Heavy industry), and LCZE (Bare rock or paved surfaces), where maximum pollutant concentrations are up to 68% higher than the overall average. However, the LCZs ranked as having the strongest overall impact on air pollution do not always correspond to those with the highest pollution levels. Feature importance analysis shows that LCZ5 (open midrise) has a significant effect on air pollution in Greater London. This is partly due to dispersion of pollutants from highly polluted areas (particularly LCZ1, LCZ2 and LCZ10 in Inner London) towards Outer Greater London, combined with emissions within LCZ5, leading to a cumulative impact on overall pollution levels. Overall, the results show the LCZ framework, despite some limitations, is a valuable approach for quantifying air pollution research, providing insights not only into the spatial distribution of high-pollution areas but also into the key factors driving urban air pollution patterns.

title: Enhancing heatwave resilience in recreational public spaces: An operational tool from a Mediterranean Algerian urban context
abstract: Heatwaves are among the most pressing climate-related challenges for contemporary cities, threatening human health, social equity, and urban infrastructure. Recreational public spaces have significant potential to enhance heatwave resilience by providing thermal refuges, supporting urban greening, and enabling social and ecological functions. However, despite growing research on urban heat, these spaces remain underexplored from an operational resilience perspective, particularly due to a lack of operational indicators and reference values for concrete evaluation and targeted improvement. To address this gap, this study introduces HResRPS - Heat Resilient Recreational Public Spaces , an operational tool designed to evaluate and enhance heatwave resilience in these spaces. Developed within an Algerian Mediterranean context, using the city of Jijel as a revealing urban laboratory experiencing increasing heatwaves, the tool translates the cyclical nature of resilience by organizing it across three hierarchical levels: phases, attributes, and operational indicators. Deep learning-based semantic clustering supported the structuring of resilience attributes, while internal consensus and a multidisciplinary Delphi-AHP process reinforced the framework’s robustness. The final tool consists of three phases, eight attribute clusters, and 22 operational indicators supported by context-adapted reference values and a composite index. HResRPS enables the assessment of overall heatwave resilience in recreational public spaces, identifies specific strengths and weaknesses across phases and attributes, and guides targeted improvement actions according to specific indicators and relevant stakeholders. It also supports new urban design projects by serving as a checklist for integrating indicators into early design stages. Finally, it offers a practical approach to sustainable and heat-resilient urban development.

title: A causal deep learning framework for simulating the thermal impact of urban land use changes
abstract: As cities face increasingly warmer conditions, exacerbated by rapid urbanization and climate change, planners lack scalable tools to predict the thermal outcomes of specific landscape interventions. This research presents a causal deep learning framework that moves beyond thermal association to simulate the counterfactual thermal impacts of urban land-use changes. Using Detroit, Michigan, as a case study, a U-Net Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was developed to estimate Land Surface Temperature (LST) by integrating 2D spatial proxies, including multi-spectral indices, albedo, and building density. The model’s performance is validated through a series of “natural experiments” using a Difference-in-Differences (DiD) logic, comparing simulated impacts with real-world land-use transitions observed between 2019 and 2025. Results indicate high predictive fidelity ( R2 of 0.95 ± 0.005, Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.404 ± 0.030 K, Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.509 ± 0.025 K) and nearly 100% accuracy in predicting the direction of thermal change across all test cases. Physical interpretability analyses via Integrated Gradients confirmed the framework learned plausible, non-linear relationships, such as cooling thresholds for vegetation and the structural shading effects of high-density urban canyons. While the model successfully isolates landscape-driven thermal signals, it exhibits a conservative bias, especially in industrial areas where anthropogenic heat is a dominant factor. This framework offers a globally scalable, data-efficient solution for cities to improve sustainability and resiliency in the face of a changing climate, providing a robust evidence base for “what-if” urban planning scenarios and proactive climate equity research.

title: Assessing the spatial distribution pattern of urban green space and its association with the hypertension prevalence rate in Beijing: A study in perspective of health benefits
abstract: ABSTRACT Urban green space (UGS) is an important component of urban landscape, the core of sustainable, ecological, livable and safe urban environment, and a key infrastructure supporting human health and well-being. Although its health benefits have been widely recognized, little is known about the relationship between the spatial distribution pattern of green spaces and health, especially in densely populated central urban areas. This study focuses on the central urban area of Beijing, relying on large health sample data, combined with green space information obtained from the GEE cloud platform, as well as data on air quality and socio-economic dynamics. Through statistical analysis, it reveals how the urban greenspace spatial pattern (UGSP) affects the hypertension prevalence rate (HPR). Research has shown that the morphology, spatial relationships, and spatial configurations of UGS exhibit significant imbalances, and there is a significant correlation and spatial correspondence between UGSP, HPR, and air quality. UGSP mainly indirectly affects residents' health through the mediating effect of air quality (CO), among which PLAND, AI, MPS, LPI, COHESION, and MSI play important roles. After integrating the above indicators, there are significant differences in HPR between sub-districts of different green space pattern categories. Therefore, based on the principle of equitable distribution, priority should be given to optimizing key pattern indicators in areas with weak green resource foundations. These findings and conclusions contribute to an understanding of the fairness of UGSP and will also guide future design and planning of UGS based on environmental health benefits.

title: Bikeability index in bike-sharing systems: A dual-level assessment integrating station accessibility and cycling environment
abstract: Understanding and improving the bikeability of urban environments is essential for advancing towards sustainable mobility and reducing the environmental burden generated by short-distance motorized travel. This study proposes a dual-level bikeability index (BI) that integrates large-scale bike-sharing trajectories, built-environment indicators, and spatial–temporal interaction patterns to evaluate urban cycling environments with high granularity and interpretability. A case study is presented using 87,855 dockless bike-sharing trips collected in Xiamen, China. We employ a residual autoencoder with Bayesian optimization to extract compact mobility embeddings that capture user behavior. Emerging hotspot analysis (EHSA) is employed to capture spatial-temporal heterogeneity, while an XGBoost model with SHAP-based interpretation is used to quantify the contributions of land-use diversity, accessibility, road network structure, and weather conditions to bikeability formation. Results show that (i) mixed-use land-use intensity, POI accessibility, and cyclable network proximity are the most influential determinants of BI; (ii) distinct temporal patterns exist between short-distance functional trips and mid-distance recreational trips; and (iii) spatial heterogeneity highlights mismatches between bike-sharing demand and infrastructure provision, particularly in mixed commercial–residential districts. Based on these findings, we provide actionable planning recommendations for station deployment, cycling network enhancement, and demand-responsive operational strategies. This research demonstrates a scalable, data-driven framework for diagnosing urban cycling environments and offers insights that can support evidence-based planning for sustainable cities.

title: Spatiotemporal variability and driving mechanisms of urban park cooling effect along an urban-rural gradient: A case study of Shanghai
abstract: Although urban parks play an important role of urban parks in mitigating the urban heat island (UHI) effect, the long-term spatiotemporal patterns and the non-linear, synergistic mechanisms driving their cooling performance across urban-rural gradients remain insufficiently quantified. This study assessed the decadal cooling effects of 210 parks within the Outer Ring Road of Shanghai using summer land surface temperatures temperature data derived from Landsat images (2016–2025). In addition, these long-term observations were interpret with a robust XGBoost-SHAP machine learning framework to explicitly interpret the multidimensional effects of park morphology and land cover. The results showed that while 97.6% of parks exhibited cooling effects during the decade, but marked interannual fluctuations limited stable annual cooling to only ∼67% of parks, and the core cooling metrics showed potential attenuation over time. Spatially, a clear trade-off was observed: parks in the peripheral Outer Ring parks achieved the mean cooling distance (174.79 m), whereas micro-parks in the Inner Ring exhibited the highest cooling efficiency (113.78 m/ha). Moreover, machine learning analysis indicated that optimal cooling is shaped by non-linear thresholds and feature interactions (e.g., Area × Tree cover). Comprehensive cooling performance was optimized when water proportions at ∼10%, building footprints were kept below 25%, and moderately complex geometries were adopted (Shape Index: 1.5–2.0), with tree cover acting as the main positive driver. Overall, this study provides precise, evidence-based thresholds for optimizing park landscape configurations, with highly efficient micro-parks prioritized in dense urban cores and large ecologically dominant parks favored in peripheral areas, to support sustained urban climate resilience.

title: Unveiling nonlinear dynamics and spatial heterogeneity in urban morphology–land surface temperature relationships: Insights from an interpretable GWRF-SHAP framework across local climate zones
abstract: Urban morphology plays a critical role in shaping urban thermal environments. However, the nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous relationships between morphological characteristics and land surface temperature (LST) remain inadequately quantified, particularly across different local climate zones (LCZs). To address this knowledge gap, this study developed an interpretable geographically weighted random forest framework integrated with SHapley Additive exPlanations (GWRF–SHAP) to evaluate the effects of 2D/3D urban morphological characteristics on block-level LST variations in Xi’an, China. Compared with the conventional RF model, the proposed GWRF model demonstrated superior predictive performance, achieving R² values of 0.718–0.719 and improving prediction accuracy by 9.2–9.9% on test datasets. The results revealed substantial spatial heterogeneity in morphology–LST relationships across LCZs. Urban compactness and imperviousness indicators, including building density (BD), floor area ratio (FAR), and the enhanced normalized difference impervious surface index (ENDISI), generally contributed to higher LSTs, whereas vegetation and water-related indicators, represented by the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and modified normalized difference water index (MNDWI), consistently exhibited cooling effects. Furthermore, pronounced nonlinear threshold effects were identified. In compact LCZs, LST increased sharply when BD exceeded approximately 0.27–0.30, while the cooling benefits of vegetation became markedly stronger only when NDVI surpassed critical thresholds ranging from 0.16 to 0.23 in open and sparsely built LCZs. In contrast, building height variability (Hstd) exhibited divergent thermal effects among LCZs, indicating strong context-dependent interactions between urban form and thermal environments. These findings highlight the value of integrating interpretable machine learning with geographically weighted modeling for uncovering complex urban morphology–LST relationships. The proposed framework provides a robust scientific basis for LCZ-specific urban heat mitigation strategies and climate-resilient urban planning.

title: Identifying potential vertical spaces for nature-based solutions in dense urban context: GeoAI approach
abstract: Cities worldwide face numerous challenges, including the urban heat island effect, urban stormwater management, and climate change. Nature-based solutions (NBS) can mitigate these impacts, while providing ecosystem services and health co-benefits, yet retrofitting NBS within dense urban fabric is difficult because suitable land is scarce. Underused or unused vertical spaces on building facades and roofs could provide opportunities to increase greenery without competing for ground-level land. However, no existing methodology simultaneously assesses both façade and rooftop vertical spaces for NBS using integrated artificial intelligence and geospatial methods; most studies focus on rooftop greening potential. In this research, we develop and evaluate an integrated GeoAI framework that combines a foundational AI segmentation model applied to street view images for façade greening assessment with a geospatial multicriteria approach for rooftop greening assessment in the dense urban context of Amsterdam. Here, greening potential refers to the physical technical feasibility based on the measurable surface areas' potential for NBS integration. When applied to street-based sampling locations in Mapillary SVI images, our framework achieved a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.74 and a mean F1 (Dice) score of 0.84 for facade segmentation, indicating high accuracy in detecting potential building façade areas. The results suggest high potential for greening building facades in predominantly residential areas, particularly in buildings with few street-facing windows. Additionally, the 10.0 km² of roof area is classified as highly suitable for green roof implementation. Spatial hotspot analysis identified several roof-greening clusters, whereas no such clustering was observed for facades. We provided a replicable workflow for broader implementation of the methodological approach in research and practice, and suggested potential future developments to further assess the vertical greening potential on the unused or underused vertical space above buildings.

title: Inferred vertical coupling of urban heat islands across morphology zones: conditional effects and planning implications
abstract: Understanding the three-dimensional structure of the urban heat island (UHI) is essential for climate-adaptive planning. Beyond surface and canopy-layer warming, UHIs involve vertically integrated heat accumulation; however, most studies assess temperature differences at a single height. This study infers vertical UHI coupling from the joint yet differentiated responses of surface (SUHII), canopy-layer (CUHII), and vertically integrated boundary-layer (VUHII) indicators, without directly quantifying coupling or simulating energy exchange. It further examines morphology-dependent relationships using morphology-zone classification and double machine learning (DML)-based statistical attribution. The results show that SUHII and CUHII exhibit continuous urban-rural gradients, whereas VUHII is more localized and fragmented. At night, mean VUHII reaches 963.5 K·m in dense central districts, compared with 206.6 K·m in peripheral plains, indicating that conventional surface- or canopy-layer metrics alone may not fully represent vertically integrated heat accumulation within the lower atmosphere. Thermal intensity generally follows high-rise compact (HC) > low-rise compact (LC) > low-rise sparse (LS) > low-rise open (LO). Nighttime VUHII trends are 59.1, 18.8, and 13.1 K·m·a⁻¹ in HC, LC, and LS zones, respectively, and winter nighttime VUHII exceeds 2500 K·m in HC zones. Transition-zone analysis indicates that VUHII changes lag behind those of SUHII and CUHII during urban-form evolution: during LS to HC transitions, VUHII remains 200–400 K·m, far below the 1500–2000 K·m observed in stable HC zones. After adjustment for observed covariates, DML-based statistical attribution indicates that land cover and surface properties have the strongest estimated conditional associations with SUHII and CUHII. In contrast, VUHII is more strongly associated with three-dimensional urban structure, atmospheric conditions, and human activity. At night, building-height heterogeneity, impervious-surface connectivity, and population density show positive conditional effects on VUHII, whereas vegetation shows a negative conditional effect. These findings provide evidence-informed planning priorities for morphology-aware mitigation of heat accumulation.

title: Urban structural and infrastructural inequalities shape fine‑scale carbon footprints of diet, housing, and transportation: Evidence from the metropolitan area of Mexico City
abstract: By 2050, over 70% of the global population will live in urban areas, mostly in the Global South. Cities account for 70–80% of global CO 2 emissions, largely from food systems, housing, and transportation. Using 992 household surveys and high‑resolution (100-m) machine learning models, we estimated spatially disaggregated per capita carbon footprints for diet, housing, and transportation across the Metropolitan Area of Mexico City (MAMC). This fine-spatial resolution uncovers emission hotspots obscured by citywide aggregates. By focusing on consumer-based spatial drivers, this study provides actionable insights for equity‑oriented climate governance. Our findings show that footprints comparable to Global North cities are driven by structural urban disparities, such as housing morphology and infrastructure access, rather than individual choices. Modelled mean annual footprints reached 10.1±1.2 tCO 2 eq with peripheral municipalities exceeding 15.0 tCO 2 eq. Dietary emissions dominated (>60%), housing contributed 10–20% but reached >40% in northern clusters, and transportation footprints were highest in sprawling, poorly connected peripheries. Emissions scaled with affluence and built-up area, whereas structural deprivation and limited access characterized low-emission peripheral zones trapped in a double burden. These findings reveal structural inequalities embedded in food, housing and mobility, deepening climate injustices and intersectional vulnerabilities across marginalized communities. Climate mitigation in Latin American must move beyond uniform mandates toward spatially targeted urban governance capable of resolving deep-seated intra-urban carbon disparities though integrated, spatially adaptive mitigation strategies. Land‑use densification, electrified transit expansion, and improved housing standards in peripheral zones offer pathways to reduce emissions while advancing urban climate justice and reducing inequality.

title: Using machine learning to unravel the driving mechanisms of carbon balance in resource-based cities: a “pattern-process-service-sustainability” framework
abstract: Resource-based cities (RBCs) have borne carbon emissions far exceeding their own development needs during rapid urbanization, making them critical areas for achieving carbon neutrality. However, existing studies have largely focused on either carbon emissions or carbon sequestration as separate processes, thereby limiting refined spatial governance. Using multi-source remote sensing data for 125 resource-based cities, this study proposes an integrated analytical framework that incorporates the Pattern-Process-Service-Sustainability (PPSS) paradigm and combines interpretable machine learning with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to identify and explain the driving mechanisms of carbon balance. The results show that, from 2002 to 2023, China’s RBCs generally remained in a state of carbon surplus, but their carbon balance declined by 69.73%, while the proportion of carbon-deficit cities increased from 28.00% to 48.80%. Spatially, carbon deficits were mainly concentrated in coal- and oil & gas-based cities in North China, whereas carbon-surplus cities were primarily distributed in forestry-based cities and cities with favorable ecological backgrounds in Northeast and Southwest China. The SHAP contribution results indicate that soil retention (SDR), green space (GS), and habitat quality (HQ) are closely associated with carbon balance and exhibit pronounced threshold effects. The PLS-SEM results further reveal that ecosystem services serve as an important link between landscape patterns and carbon balance. Rather than exerting a simple linear influence, landscape patterns mainly affect carbon balance indirectly through the “pattern-process-service” pathway. These findings provide a theoretical framework and methodological reference for optimizing source-sink spatial configurations and formulating differentiated carbon-neutrality strategies in resource-based cities.

title: From energy efficiency to thermal resilience and passive survivability during summer power outages: AI-supported prediction and physics-based genetic algorithm optimization of building envelopes
abstract: Climate change and extreme weather events are intensifying the vulnerability of existing buildings to energy system failures, especially during prolonged heat waves. Power outages under such conditions compromise occupant health, and impose economic burdens. While resilience research has traditionally focused on energy infrastructure, the role of building envelopes in maintaining habitable indoor conditions during outages has been underexplored. This study presents a BIM-based simulation framework that couples AI prediction with multi-objective genetic algorithm optimization for evaluating and optimizing building envelope energy retrofits to enhance thermal resilience in residential buildings. Four representative housing typologies including detached, semi-detached, attached, and mid-rise apartments, were modeled across 14 ASHRAE climate zones. A dataset of 16,856 EnergyPlus simulations was generated using Latin Hypercube Sampling, capturing a wide spectrum of building envelope energy retrofits for walls, roofs, floors, and windows. Thermal resilience was evaluated through a suite of indicators, including Passive Survivability Index (PSI), Time to Thermal Failure, Temperature Deviation, Humidity Exposure Risk, Recovery Time, Post-outage Recovery Load, and Weighted Unmet Temperature Penalty ( WUMT P t ). XGBoost was trained on this dataset to predict thermal resilience metrics with high accuracy, enabling scalable and automated assessment. Finally, multi-objective optimization using NSGA-II identified Pareto-optimal retrofit solutions balancing survivability, thermal comfort, and energy recovery needs across climates. Results indicate that envelope retrofit strategies increased the average PSI during multi-day summer power outages by 14.9 percentage points across the evaluated climate zones and building typologies, corresponding to a 72.1% relative improvement. At the individual-case level, PSI improved by up to 54.7 percentage points (298%), thermal failure was delayed by up to 25 hours (261%), WUMT P t decreased by up to 145.6 points (63%), and peak indoor temperatures decreased by up to 8.3°C relative to baseline configurations. AI-based prediction achieved an overall R² above 0.99 for time-series outputs and 0.81 for static resilience metrics, with individual static-metric R² values ranging from 0.66 to 0.95, enabling rapid screening of retrofit options and supporting informed decision-making. Multi-objective optimization revealed clear trade-offs between passive survivability and energy performance, identifying Pareto-optimal retrofit packages tailored to climate and housing type. This study demonstrates that resilience-oriented envelope retrofits can improve occupant safety during outages, providing actionable guidance for climate-adaptive residential energy retrofit planning.

title: Machine learning for climate-responsive urban design and planning: a scoping review
abstract: Urban climate researchers increasingly use machine learning (ML) to examine microclimate conditions and their effects on comfort, health, and energy. Findings from these studies increasingly inform architecture, urban design, planning, and policy. However, how these approaches translate into usable knowledge for spatial decision-making in the built environment remains uncertain. This scoping review, conducted following PRISMA-ScR, examines 211 applied studies that use ML to relate urban form and environmental conditions to microclimatic outcomes across multiple spatial scales, from façade-level performance and street canyons to neighborhood patterns and city-wide assessments. Based on this literature, this review is organized into four principal application domains: (1) association and influence analysis, (2) classification and clustering, (3) data augmentation, and (4) forecasting and simulation. Across these domains, ML is used to identify relationships between built form and environmental conditions, group similar urban situations, extend incomplete datasets, and support predictive analysis relevant to planning and intervention. Several recurring limitations emerge when these studies are considered from the standpoint of practice. Many models are developed and tested within a single empirical setting, and studies rarely show whether the same relationships hold in other urban contexts. Data coverage and representativeness are also often unclear. In addition, urban form is frequently described using simplified indicators that miss geometric detail and typological differences relevant to climate-sensitive design. As a result, ML applications in urban microclimate research currently work best as tools for pattern recognition and exploratory analysis, while their use as a basis for robust design guidance or broadly applicable planning strategies remains more limited. To overcome the limitations, the review outlines a set of cross-context validation principles for researchers and practitioners.

title: Learning dependency structures of urban vitality at the census-block level using Bayesian networks and multi-source data
abstract: ABSTRACT Urban vitality captures the dynamic interplay between human activity and the built environment, serving as a critical metric for guiding urban planning and design toward more livable, inclusive, and resilient cities. However, existing studies have largely overlooked the underlying dependency relationships shaping urban vitality, particularly when analyzing large-scale and multi-source urban data. To address this gap, this study proposes a data-driven framework to model and interpret urban vitality intensity at the census-block level in Manhattan, New York. Within this framework, a composite Urban Vitality Index (UVI) is first constructed by integrating dynamic and static proxies of urban activity, derived from street-level imagery–based object detection and POI density, respectively. Second, sixteen influencing factors spanning neighborhood attributes, urban form, building form, and environmental perception are incorporated to represent multi-dimensional characteristics of the urban system. Third, a Bayesian Network is employed to capture the dependency structure, revealing probabilistic relationships and underlying pathways associated with urban vitality and its influencing factors. The results indicate that socio-spatial factors, particularly ethnic diversity and road network density, are strongly associated with urban vitality through interconnected pathways, whereas localized morphological characteristics exhibit comparatively weaker effects. By leveraging deep learning and interpretable probabilistic modeling, this study facilitates knowledge discovery in urban systems, providing a scalable approach for evidence-based urban planning and design.

title: VisionMRT: Physics-based outdoor thermal exposure and comfort modeling using photographs and 3D reconstruction
abstract: Urban overheating is an escalating global challenge with severe consequences for public health, livability, and infrastructure resilience. Assessing human thermal exposure at pedestrian-relevant scales is critical for designing heat-resilient cities, but existing approaches often rely on specialized instrumentation or computationally intensive simulations that limit broader use. We introduce VisionMRT, an open-source, image-based modeling framework for estimating outdoor thermal exposure from pedestrian-level photos and standard meteorological inputs. VisionMRT integrates computer vision and physics-informed radiative modeling within a generalizable workflow. The tool uses six-directional cube-map imagery to classify urban surface types through semantic segmentation and reconstruct local geometry through monocular depth estimation. These image-derived inputs are used to generate shadow maps, estimate sky view factor from hemispherical projections, compute surface temperatures using a physics-based surface energy balance, and integrate directional shortwave and longwave radiative fluxes. The framework estimates Mean Radiant Temperature (MRT), a key determinant of outdoor heat exposure, and two indices: Physiological Equivalent Temperature (PET), and Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI). We validated VisionMRT against observations from the MaRTy biometeorological platform collected during summer across 132 sites in the Phoenix metropolitan area, Arizona, USA. VisionMRT achieved an MRT RMSE of 3.12°C, an MAE of 2.61°C, an MBE of -0.26°C, and an R² of 0.94 across 1,174 data records with diverse urban morphologies and shading conditions. Since the model relies on widely available imagery, standard meteorological data, and open-source methods, VisionMRT offers a scalable and transferable approach for pedestrian-scale heat exposure assessment, urban design evaluation, and climate adaptation planning.
